items.stem: Which of the following best describes "HL essay criteria"?
options: A Knowledge, understanding and interpretation; B Analysis and evaluation; C Focus, organisation and development; D Language – 5 marks each, 20 total
The alphabetical list of sources at the end of an essay in MLA style
A referencing system (Modern Language Association) commonly used in literary studies, with in-text citations and a works-cited list
A complete version of the essay submitted for teacher feedback before the final version
items.answer: A Knowledge, understanding and interpretation; B Analysis and evaluation; C Focus, organisation and development; D Language – 5 marks each, 20 total
items.markingKey: A. "HL essay criteria" is A Knowledge, understanding and interpretation; B Analysis and evaluation; C Focus, organisation and development; D Language – 5 marks each, 20 total.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a thesis and a line of inquiry.
items.answer: A line of inquiry is the question the essay investigates; the thesis is the essay's arguable answer to it.
items.markingKey: A line of inquiry is the question the essay investigates; the thesis is the essay's arguable answer to it. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "An HL essay conclusion should just repeat the thesis." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: A conclusion should synthesise how the sections answer the inquiry and evaluate the significance of the findings.
items.markingKey: A conclusion should synthesise how the sections answer the inquiry and evaluate the significance of the findings. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: For the HL essay question "How does Satrapi use the visual representation of the veil to explore the construction of Marji's identity?", propose an arguable thesis and explain which evidence from Marjane Satrapi's Persepolis you would use.
items.answer: Model thesis: Satrapi's repeated, stylised images of the veil turn a garment into a contested sign, tracing Marji's identity as something imposed, resisted and finally chosen. Sections should each analyse specific authorial choices in Marjane Satrapi's Persepolis that support the thesis, ending with evaluation.
items.markingKey: Model thesis: Satrapi's repeated, stylised images of the veil turn a garment into a contested sign, tracing Marji's identity as something imposed, resisted and finally chosen. Sections should each analyse specific authorial choices in Marjane Satrapi's Persepolis that support the thesis, ending with evaluation.

items.stem: Explain how the line of inquiry "How do parody advertisements transform the conventions of fashion advertising to expose the hidden costs of fast fashion?" connects to the course concept of transformation, and how you would structure a 1,200–1,500-word essay on it.
items.answer: Indicative content: context of the work; clear statement of the line of inquiry; thesis such as "The parodies keep the visual grammar of glossy adverts but subvert slogans and small print, making the genre confess what it normally hides."; outline of argument; link to transformation. HL essay criteria (5 marks each): A knowledge, understanding and interpretation; B analysis and evaluation; C focus, organisation and development; D language.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: context of the work; clear statement of the line of inquiry; thesis such as "The parodies keep the visual grammar of glossy adverts but subvert slogans and small print, making the genre confess what it normally hides."; outline of argument; link to transformation. HL essay criteria (5 marks each): A knowledge, understanding and interpretation; B analysis and evaluation; C focus, organisation and development; D language.

items.stem: Allocate 1,400 words across the sections of an HL essay and justify the allocation.
items.answer: For example: introduction about 150; three body sections about 350 each; conclusion about 150; justification based on analysis weight.
items.markingKey: For example: introduction about 150; three body sections about 350 each; conclusion about 150; justification based on analysis weight.

items.stem: Write a detailed plan for a 1,200–1,500-word HL essay, including thesis, section topics, evidence and word allocation.
items.answer: Indicative content: focused thesis; argument-led sections; specific evidence; realistic word allocation.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: focused thesis; argument-led sections; specific evidence; realistic word allocation.

items.stem: "A strong conclusion can significantly raise an HL essay's mark." Discuss.
items.answer: A strong conclusion helps criteria C and B but cannot compensate for weak body sections.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it shows synthesis and evaluation; it leaves a final impression. Arguments against: marks depend mainly on analysis in the body; a conclusion cannot rescue weak analysis. Supported judgement: A strong conclusion helps criteria C and B but cannot compensate for weak body sections. Markbands (10 marks): Markbands (criteria A–D). A Knowledge, understanding and interpretation; B Analysis and evaluation of authorial choices; C Focus and organisation; D Language. Top band: an insightful, convincing interpretation supported by well-chosen references; perceptive analysis of how specific choices shape meaning and affect the audience; a sustained, coherent line of argument; precise, varied, register-appropriate academic language. Middle band: relevant interpretation and some analysis, but partly descriptive or unevenly supported. Low band: mostly summary or feature-spotting without effect.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the HL essay thesis should appear early.
items.answer: Stating the thesis in the introduction gives the reader the line of argument from the start and lets each section be judged against it (criterion C).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Stating the thesis in the introduction gives the reader the line of argument from the start and lets each section be judged against it (criterion C). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: In MLA style, the list of sources at the end of an essay is called:
items.answer: Works Cited
items.markingKey: Works Cited. MLA uses "Works Cited".

items.stem: Explain why embedded quotations are preferable to long block quotations in the HL essay.
items.answer: They save words, allow close analysis of key words and keep the student's argument in control.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They save words, allow close analysis of key words and keep the student's argument in control. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between a works-cited entry and an in-text citation.
items.answer: An in-text citation is a short reference within the essay (author and page); a works-cited entry gives full publication details at the end.
items.markingKey: An in-text citation is a short reference within the essay (author and page); a works-cited entry gives full publication details at the end. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: For the HL essay question "How does Atwood use the "Historical Notes" epilogue to question the reliability and authority of Offred's testimony?", propose an arguable thesis and explain which evidence from Margaret Atwood's The Handmaid's Tale you would use.
items.answer: Model thesis: Atwood's epilogue reframes Offred's narrative as an academic artefact, exposing how male scholars reduce testimony to evidence and inviting the reader to resist that reduction. Sections should each analyse specific authorial choices in Margaret Atwood's The Handmaid's Tale that support the thesis, ending with evaluation.
items.markingKey: Model thesis: Atwood's epilogue reframes Offred's narrative as an academic artefact, exposing how male scholars reduce testimony to evidence and inviting the reader to resist that reduction. Sections should each analyse specific authorial choices in Margaret Atwood's The Handmaid's Tale that support the thesis, ending with evaluation.

items.stem: "Quotations from the primary text do not need to be cited." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: All quotations, including from the primary text, should be referenced so that the reader can locate them.
items.markingKey: All quotations, including from the primary text, should be referenced so that the reader can locate them. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Referencing style matters less than the quality of the analysis."
items.answer: Analysis carries most marks, but correct referencing is essential for integrity and clarity.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: criteria reward analysis mostly; minor formatting errors rarely change bands. Arguments against: referencing is part of academic integrity; poor referencing undermines credibility. Supported judgement: Analysis carries most marks, but correct referencing is essential for integrity and clarity.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "embedded quotation".
items.answer: A quotation integrated grammatically into the student's sentence
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a quotation integrated grammatically into the student's sentence. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.answer: An in-text citation is a short reference within the essay (author and page); a works-cited entry gives full publication details at the end.
items.markingKey: An in-text citation is a short reference within the essay (author and page); a works-cited entry gives full publication details at the end. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Rewrite this sentence with an embedded quotation and MLA citation: The narrator says that the women sat on one side. (page 54, author Roy)
items.answer: Example: The narrator observes that the women "sat on one side" (Roy 54), a spatial division that mirrors the novel's social boundaries. (Credit any accurate embedding and citation format.)
items.markingKey: Example: The narrator observes that the women "sat on one side" (Roy 54), a spatial division that mirrors the novel's social boundaries. (Credit any accurate embedding and citation format.)

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "redrafting"?
options: A brief reference in the text, e.g. (Achebe 208), pointing to the full entry in the works cited
Revising the essay in response to feedback and self-assessment
A Knowledge, understanding and interpretation; B Analysis and evaluation; C Focus, organisation and development; D Language – 5 marks each, 20 total
The final section that synthesises the argument and evaluates its significance
items.answer: Revising the essay in response to feedback and self-assessment
items.markingKey: B. "redrafting" is revising the essay in response to feedback and self-assessment.

items.stem: "The teacher can correct the HL essay draft line by line." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: IB rules allow only general feedback on one draft; teachers must not edit the work.
items.markingKey: IB rules allow only general feedback on one draft; teachers must not edit the work. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why self-assessment against criteria A–D is useful before redrafting.
items.answer: It helps the student identify specific weaknesses (focus, analysis, language) and plan targeted revisions. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It helps the student identify specific weaknesses (focus, analysis, language) and plan targeted revisions. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Evaluate the suitability of this HL essay line of inquiry: "Why does Nora leave?" (text: Henrik Ibsen's A Doll's House (in translation)). Suggest an improved version.
items.answer: Weak: it is too broad, invites summary or opinion and does not focus on authorial choices or a course concept. Improved: "How does Ibsen use stage props such as the macaroons, the Christmas tree and the letterbox to trace Nora's changing sense of self?" (linked to identity).
items.markingKey: Weak: it is too broad, invites summary or opinion and does not focus on authorial choices or a course concept. Improved: "How does Ibsen use stage props such as the macaroons, the Christmas tree and the letterbox to trace Nora's changing sense of self?" (linked to identity).

items.stem: A draft scores well on criterion D but often summarises the plot. Which criterion should the student target and how?
items.answer: Criterion B (and A); replace summary with analysis of authorial choices and their effects, using short embedded quotations.
items.markingKey: Criterion B (and A); replace summary with analysis of authorial choices and their effects, using short embedded quotations.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "The first draft of an HL essay matters more than the final draft."
items.answer: The first draft is crucial for useful feedback, but the final draft is what is assessed.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: feedback depends on a complete draft; early structure shapes the essay. Arguments against: only the final version is assessed; major revisions are possible. Supported judgement: The first draft is crucial for useful feedback, but the final draft is what is assessed.

items.stem: Teacher feedback on the HL essay draft may:
options: Correct every error
Award a final mark
Rewrite weak paragraphs
Give general comments but not edit or correct the text
items.answer: Give general comments but not edit or correct the text
items.markingKey: D. Feedback must be general.

items.stem: Teacher feedback says: "Your analysis is strong but your sections do not connect clearly to your line of inquiry." Which criterion is affected and what two revisions would you make?
items.answer: Criterion C; add topic sentences that link each section to the line of inquiry and transitions showing how each section develops the argument; revise the conclusion to synthesise.
items.markingKey: Criterion C; add topic sentences that link each section to the line of inquiry and transitions showing how each section develops the argument; revise the conclusion to synthesise.

items.stem: Write a redrafting plan for an HL essay draft, identifying three targets linked to specific criteria and the changes you would make.
items.answer: Indicative content: targets linked to A–D; specific revisions; prioritisation.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: targets linked to A–D; specific revisions; prioritisation.

items.stem: How many marks is the HL essay worth?
items.markingKey: D. Four criteria × 5 marks.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The alphabetical list of sources at the end of an essay in MLA style"?
options: final submission
works cited
in-text citation
embedded quotation
items.answer: works cited
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of works cited.

items.stem: Distinguish between proofreading and revising.
items.answer: Revising changes content and structure to improve the argument; proofreading corrects surface errors in spelling, grammar and punctuation.
items.markingKey: Revising changes content and structure to improve the argument; proofreading corrects surface errors in spelling, grammar and punctuation. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why each body section of the HL essay should advance the argument.
items.answer: Criterion C rewards development; sections that build on each other show a coherent, progressing argument.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Criterion C rewards development; sections that build on each other show a coherent, progressing argument. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why consistent referencing matters.
items.answer: It shows academic integrity and allows the reader to locate evidence; inconsistency suggests carelessness.

items.stem: Explain why redrafting should focus on the argument rather than only on surface errors.
items.answer: Most marks depend on interpretation, analysis and organisation; fixing these has more impact than correcting typos.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Most marks depend on interpretation, analysis and organisation; fixing these has more impact than correcting typos. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why the HL essay should analyse rather than summarise.
items.answer: The examiner knows the work; criterion B rewards analysis of authorial choices, while summary uses words without earning marks.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The examiner knows the work; criterion B rewards analysis of authorial choices, while summary uses words without earning marks. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
HL essay line of inquiry: "In what ways does Achebe's ending, narrated from the District Commissioner's perspective, critique colonial representations of Africa?"
Write a thesis statement for this essay and outline three sections that would develop it.
items.answer: Model thesis: The sudden shift to the Commissioner's view, and his plan to reduce Okonkwo to "a reasonable paragraph", exposes how colonial writing erased the complexity the novel has shown. Sections should each analyse specific authorial choices in Chinua Achebe's Things Fall Apart that support the thesis, ending with evaluation.
